Adaptivity has attained much attention in the online learning literature over the years (an incomplete list includes Herbster and Warmuth (1998); Bousquet and Warmuth (2003); Blum and Mansour (2007); Hazan and Seshadhri (2007); Kapralov and Panigrahy (2011); Cesa- Bianchi et al. (2012); Adamskiy et al. (2012); Panigrahy and Popat (2013); Luo and Schapire (2015); Daniely et al. (2015); Altschuler and Talwar (2018). Another related, but somewhat orthogonal line of work Zinkevich (2003); Hall and Willett (2013); Rakhlin and Sridharan (2013); Jadbabaie et al. (2015) studies drifting environments. Switching costs were studied in Kalai and Vempala (2005) and attained considerable interest recently (e.g, Geulen et al. (2010); Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2013); Dekel et al. (2014)). Connections between regret-minimization and competitiveness has been previously studied. In particular Blum et al. (2002); Blum and Burch (2000); Abernethy et al. (2010); Buchbinder et al. (2012) focus on algorithmic techniques that simultaneously apply to MTS and experts, and also show regret minimization algorithms for MTS an other online problems. Another example is Andrew et al. (2013) that studies tradeoffs between regret minimization and competitiveness for a certain online convex problem. Technically, the work of Kapralov and Panigrahy (2011) is quite close to our work. They showed an algorithm for the two experts √ problem that has essentially no regret w.r.t. one of the experts, and nearly optimal regret (Õ( T )) w.r.t. the second expert. They also showed that this result implies an algorithm with strongly adaptive guarantees in the N -experts problem. Namely, they showed an algorithm with nearly optimal regret on every geometric time interval. Our main contribution, regarding regret minimization, is to handle switching costs. In addition, we extend the regret bound to hold on all intervals.

context: Maybe the most interesting and fruitful direction is to find other online problems that can fall into our framework and for which we can develop computationally efficient online algorithms. We believe that our results can be extended the many other online problems such as competitive data structures (see Blum et al. (2002) for results in this direction), buffering, scheduling, load balancing, etc. Likewise, our expert results can be extended to other settings such as partial information models3 , strategic environments, non-oblivious adversaries, etc. In our approach there is a design issue of selecting the benchmark to consider. We have taken probably the most obvious benchmark, an online algorithm that does not change its state, however, one can consider other benchmarks which are more problem specific. In addition to this grand challenge, there are also open problems regarding our specific analysis.
